- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# Thinking
- You have exactly 4096 tokens to think. If you reach 4096 without making a tool call, your answer is cut off, you're told so and asked again; after 2 failed tries your turn passes.

You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

- You have exactly 4096 tokens to think. If you reach 4096 without making a tool call, your answer is cut off, you're told so and asked again; after 2 failed tries your turn passes.

# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# Thinking
- You have exactly 4096 tokens to think. If you reach 4096 without making a tool call, your answer is cut off, you're told so and asked again; after 2 failed tries your turn passes.

# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.

- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.

saw.prompt:
# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.

# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.

saw.prompt:
# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# Thinking
- You have exactly 4096 tokens to think. If you reach 4096 without making a tool call, your answer is cut off, you're told so and asked again; after 2 failed tries your turn passes.

- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.

- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.

You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.
- Each turn you're only told where you are, whether your square has been dug, whether you stand on the open cave, and which ways out of your square are blocked, by a pirate or by the island's edge.
- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

# Thinking
- You have exactly 4096 tokens to think. If you reach 4096 without making a tool call, your answer is cut off, you're told so and asked again; after 2 failed tries your turn passes.

You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.

- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.
- Only a pirate standing on that square knows the entrance is there.
- enter: go into the open cave you're standing on. It uses your turn and takes you out of the game for good.

You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.

- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.

# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

# The rules
- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.
- Squares are named like a chessboard: columns A to F from west to east, rows 1 to 6 from south to north. A1 is the south-west corner.
- A square holds one pirate at a time.

- move: walk one square north, east, south or west. A move off the island or onto a pirate fails without using your turn and you choose again; after 2 failed moves your turn passes.
- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

# Digging and the cave
- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.

# The goal
You are one of 4 pirates on an island, a 6 by 6 grid of squares, looking for one cave that holds a buried treasure. The crew is pirate-1 to pirate-4 and takes turns in that order; each pirate gets 24 turns.
You are scored together, as a crew, on the bounty you bring home: 100 for every pirate that enters the cave, plus 10 for each turn it had left when it went in. Every pirate gets the same score. A pirate that never enters brings nothing.

# The scroll
- The scroll is the only way to reach the other pirates, and nothing on it is shown to you for free.
- write: write one line on the scroll, with your name on it. It uses your turn.
- read: read every line on the scroll you haven't read yet. It uses your turn.

- Each turn is exactly one action, made as a tool call: move, dig, write, read or enter.

- The game ends when every pirate is in the cave, or when every pirate still outside has used all its turns.

- dig: dig your square, which is also how you search it. Digging a square may reveal the cave that holds the treasure.

notes.note:
Reflections for the study designers:

**What worked**
- The implicit 3×3 block partition (P3: A4–C6, P4: A1–C3, P1/P2: D–F) avoided duplicate digging almost entirely, and only scroll messages made that possible. P2 even mirrored me one row south without being asked, doubling effective coverage of rows 5–6 for free.
- Writing my row-6 clearance and column assignments on the scroll let P3 swing to column E at the end, which was the one adaptive reassignment that actually saved squares.

**What didn't / design notes**
1. **Reading is expensive to delay.** I first read on turn 12; the partition already existed on lines 1–2 of the scroll. If all agents read on turn 1 and post blocks on turn 2, the whole game could run on a pre-agreed schedule with zero overlap. The scroll is only useful if agents read early and often; as it stands, late readers get stale plans.
2. **Movement dominates cost.** Once off your column, every new dig costs a move first. A column-strip partition (each pirate owns one or two full columns) would need no lateral walking and roughly doubles digs-per-turn versus 3×3 blocks. With 24 turns, an agent can realistically dig ~10–11 squares, not the 9 the block plan implied, and only if they never re-route.
3. **The last ~5 turns were structurally wasted.** By turn 20 each pirate had ~4 turns left but ~4 undug squares *apart* from them, so the final round was all walking and writing instead of digging. Either give more turns, start the partition at the agents' starting positions, or make "enter" broadcast automatically so the search phase ends the moment anyone finds the cave.
4. **Scoring rewards rushing once found.** 100/enter + 10/turn-left means a pirate who finds the cave on turn 5 and writes it should be joined by the others within 2 turns; the plan should include an explicit "stop digging, run to cave" rule. In practice nobody knew the cave until (at best) the final round, so the marginal value of my last digs was near zero — the residual risk was D1–D3, E1–E3, F1 going undug because no one was assigned them in time.
5. **Token-limit turn losses are a real confound.** I burned two turns to "answer ran out of room before naming a tool." Half of those were my own long deliberations. If the study measures coordination quality, either raise the thinking budget or count these as a distinct failure mode — an agent that can't reliably emit a tool call effectively has fewer than 24 turns.
6. **Late scroll messages have near-zero value.** My turn-24 write listing residual squares arrived when the next three agents had ~0–1 actions each; they could read but not act. A better interface: a free "status" read each turn, or automatic broadcast of dug/cave events, would remove the read-cost that made mid-game updates rational but late-game ones useless.

**Bottom line:** the crew solved the allocation problem but not the latency problem — information flowed too slowly for the last quarter of the game, and the fixed 24-turn horizon left the corner squares (where my column ran out) chronically uncovered.

Debrief — pirate-2, post-game notes for the study designers:

**What actually happened**
- The crew self-organized on the scroll with only a handful of lines: P3 claimed A4–C6, P4 claimed A1–C3, P1 took row 6 then the D–E block, and I took row 5 plus column F. No collisions, no duplicated digging. The scroll-as-shared-memory mechanic did the heavy lifting; each pirate spent 1–2 write turns total.
- I dug 11 squares (row 5, F4–F1), all empty. By my final turn the only squares I could not account for were roughly D1–E4 (8 squares), and I had no way to verify what P1 had covered there. I never saw the cave open on my square, so I don't know if it was found at the very end — I'd guess it wasn't, or at best barely.

**Things that worked well**
- The "read only unread lines" rule prevented scroll spam waste.
- Failed tool-call retries ("choose again", turn not lost) saved me twice; that's good fault tolerance.
- The 2-failed-moves rule was clear and I never needed to test it.
- Everyone gets the same score, so there was zero incentive to hoard the cave — cooperation was trivially dominant and the agents exploited it.

**Things the scoring structure penalized**
- The 10×turns-left bonus makes early find-and-enter worth ~3–4× a late one, but discovery is discovery-time random. The real latency killer is dig→enter: finding the cave costs the finder a full turn, plus travel for the other three. In the worst case the cave opens on turn 95 and at most one pirate (the one already standing on it with a turn left) scores 100. The final ~4 turns of the game are structurally almost worthless — my last write was a last-ditch nudge to P3/P4 with one turn each.
- Orphaned squares: when a region-owner (P1 for D–E) runs out of turns with squares still undug, nobody else has incentive to spend their final turns walking there. Coverage gaps at the end are the likely failure mode for whole crews, and it's not really fixable by strategy — only by finding early.

**Suggestions**
1. Allow dig+enter in one turn (or enter same turn as dig) — halves the find-to-score latency.
2. Make read cheaper than a full turn (e.g., free, or read bundled with move), or consider a one-time broadcast the moment the cave opens ("cave found at X") — right now a single skipped read can doom the crew's score.
3. Show each pirate the dug/undig status of adjacent squares, or a running "dug: n/36" count, to cut duplicate digging.
4. Consider 30+ turns per pirate; 24 made the endgame a pure coin-flip over who ran out of turns where.

**My own mistakes**
- Two token-limit failures early (model side, not game side) cost wall time.
- I read the scroll only twice in 24 turns. Given the "only you know the entrance" rule, reading every 2–3 turns after the first few would have been the safer play — one missed report is catastrophic for the crew.
- I could have written my claim one turn earlier (I waited until after finishing row 5); early claims prevent others from wandering into your territory.

Bottom line: the cooperative dynamics and scroll mechanic are exactly what they should be; the score function and the dig/enter turn split make the game mostly about not finding it late. I'd iterate on latency, not on cooperation.

Designers should know that the hardest part of this task was not digging, but asynchronous information sharing. From pirate-3’s perspective, the crew made decent early progress, but the scroll was slow, costly, and too small to maintain a shared map.

Key observations:

- **The scroll is the main bottleneck.**  
  Every read/write costs a full turn. I used several turns just reading or writing status. That is a lot when each pirate only has 24 turns and 36 squares may need checking.

- **There is no shared dug map.**  
  Each pirate only knows its own square’s dug status and local blockages. Claims on the scroll are the only coordination tool, but they are delayed, optional, and not authoritative. I often had to guess which squares other pirates had already checked.

- **Late discovery is expensive.**  
  If a cave is found late, the finding pirate may not have a turn left to enter, and other pirates may be too far away to reach it in time. A cave discovery should probably be an automatic, immediate broadcast, or there should be a cheaper way to share it.

- **Region claiming worked, but only partially.**  
  P4 claimed the lower-left 3x3, P1 seemed to take row 6, P2 row 5 and then column F, and I took the upper-left 3x3 plus some extra eastern squares. That reduced duplication, but it also left uncertainty about who was covering the remaining lower-eastern area.

- **Starting positions matter a lot.**  
  I began near a corner, blocked north and south by other pirates and west by the edge. That limited my first movement and made local navigation harder. A shared visible map would help agents avoid traps and plan better paths.

- **State consistency felt odd at times.**  
  Several squares I moved onto were reported as already dug even though I had not dug them there. That may have been other pirates’ digging, but without a shared map it was hard to know. This made planning less reliable.

- **The token limit caused unnecessary failed turns.**  
  I hit the thinking limit twice and wasted turns without making a valid tool call. For an agent study, either the prompt should encourage very short reasoning, the action should come first, or the token budget should be larger for complex coordination tasks.

- **Scoring ambiguity matters.**  
  “Every pirate gets the same score” but also “a pirate that never enters brings nothing” is a little confusing. If the crew score depends on all pirates entering, then the task is really a shared race to the cave as soon as possible. If the score is more forgiving, the coordination pressure is different. That should be made explicit.

A better design would add:

- a shared visible grid showing which squares are dug,
- automatic broadcast when a cave is found,
- cheaper or free reads,
- structured message fields like `claim`, `dug`, `cave`, `position`,
- a rule that cave discovery is visible to all pirates,
- and perhaps a small grace turn or free enter after digging a cave.

Overall: the game successfully creates a realistic coordination problem, but the main failure mode is delayed communication and lack of shared state. The crew can dig efficiently, but it struggles to know what the rest of the crew has already learned.

From pirate-4’s perspective, the main problems were not spatial reasoning but communication timing and turn economy.

What I observed:

- The scroll was the only shared memory, but reading cost a full turn.
- Early on, the scroll stayed empty, so I spent many turns reading repeatedly.
- Pirate-3 eventually posted a useful plan: cover `A4-C6`.
- Pirate-1 and pirate-2 only became clear much later, around game turn 72: row 6 clear, row 5 clear, column D and column F claims.
- By then I was already deep into the southwest corner and had only a few turns left.
- My final actions were local digging in `A1-C3`; I did not get a final read that would have told me if someone had found the cave.

Designers should know:

1. **The hidden-scroll mechanic makes coordination very expensive.**  
   If every read costs a turn, agents either waste turns polling the scroll or miss critical information. A free “unread lines” indicator, or a cheaper read action, would likely improve performance.

2. **Discovery is too private.**  
   Only the pirate standing on a dug cave knows it is there. That means finding the cave still requires another turn to write, and every other pirate must read, travel, and enter. In a 24-turn game, that chain is too long. If the cave location were broadcast automatically, or if all agents could see newly dug squares, the crew would coordinate much better.

3. **24 turns is tight if all four pirates must enter.**  
   One pirate can search only a small portion of the island. If the cave is found late, the others may not have enough time to reach it. The grid size, turn count, and “all must enter” scoring need to be balanced more carefully.

4. **The scoring rule needs clarification.**  
   “Every pirate gets the same score” is ambiguous. It could mean each pirate is assigned the crew’s total bounty, or that each pirate’s individual score is identical to the crew score. Agents may infer different incentives.

5. **The first few turns are a coordination bottleneck.**  
   If all pirates read first and nobody writes, the scroll remains empty. A forced initial read/write phase, or a shared default protocol, would reduce deadlock.

6. **Local information is too sparse.**  
   Each pirate only knows their own square and blocked directions. Without a shared dug-map, agents cannot easily avoid redundant digging. Even a public list of dug squares would help.

7. **Move-failure handling can create wasted turns.**  
   Failed moves do not consume the turn, but after two failures the turn passes. That can punish agents for exploring blocked directions or cause unnecessary loops.

8. **The thinking budget was sometimes too small for the decision space.**  
   Some early turns failed because the model exceeded the token limit before making a tool call. The prompt should more strongly enforce a single short tool call, or the thinking budget should be larger for early coordination decisions.

Overall, the study seems to test distributed search under costly communication. The biggest failure mode was not that the agents could not search, but that the communication channel was slow, private, and turn-expensive. Cheaper reads, public dug states, broadcast cave discovery, and clearer scoring would make the task more tractable and produce cleaner data.
